what_its_for: Melatonin is a natural hormone your body already makes to help you sleep. As a supplement, it is used to help you fall asleep faster, especially if you have trouble sleeping (insomnia), are adjusting to shift work, or are dealing with jet lag from traveling across time zones.
how_to_take: Take melatonin by mouth about 30 to 60 minutes before you plan to go to sleep. Swallow tablets or capsules whole with a glass of water. If you are using a liquid form, measure the dose carefully with the dropper or measuring cup provided. Sublingual tablets (the kind that dissolve under your tongue) should be placed under your tongue and allowed to dissolve — do not swallow them whole. You can take melatonin with or without food, but avoid taking it with a heavy or fatty meal.
dosing: For most adults, a dose of 0.5 mg to 5 mg taken 30 to 60 minutes before bedtime is a good starting point. Many people start with the lowest effective dose (0.5 mg to 1 mg) and increase slowly only if needed. For jet lag, take 0.5 mg to 5 mg at bedtime on the day you arrive at your destination and continue for 2 to 5 days. Do not take more than 10 mg in a 24-hour period unless your doctor tells you to. Always follow the label directions or your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: Melatonin is usually taken only when needed, so a traditional missed dose schedule does not apply. If you forget to take it before bed and you are still planning to sleep, you may take it if you still have at least 4 to 6 hours left before you need to wake up. If it is almost time to get up, skip the dose. Never double up to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store melatonin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight, heat, and moisture — do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed and out of reach of children and pets. Check the expiration date on the package and do not use it after that date.
what_to_avoid: Avoid alcohol while taking melatonin, as it can increase drowsiness and make side effects worse. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert for at least 4 to 5 hours after taking melatonin. Avoid bright light, especially blue light from phones, tablets, and computer screens, after taking melatonin, as light can block its effects. Avoid caffeine close to bedtime. Do not combine melatonin with other sleep aids, sedatives, or anti-anxiety medications without first talking to your doctor or pharmacist.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or pharmacist if you experience unusual or severe drowsiness the next morning, headaches, dizziness, nausea, or irritability that does not go away. Contact your doctor if your sleep problems last longer than 2 weeks, as ongoing insomnia may be a sign of another medical condition. Also call your doctor if you are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before using melatonin. Seek emergency help immediately if you have signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Melatonin usually begins to make you feel sleepy within 30 to 60 minutes after taking it. For jet lag, you may notice improvement in your sleep pattern within 2 to 5 days of use. For general sleep problems, you may see improvement within a few days to a couple of weeks. If you do not notice any benefit after 1 to 2 weeks of regular use, speak with your doctor about other options.
special_populations: Children: Melatonin is sometimes used in children with sleep disorders, especially in children with ADHD or autism spectrum disorder, but only under the guidance of a pediatrician. Use the lowest effective dose and do not give it to children long-term without medical supervision. Older Adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to melatonin and should start with the lowest dose possible (0.5 mg) to reduce the risk of morning grogginess, falls, or confusion. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: The safety of melatonin during pregnancy or breastfeeding has not been well studied. Avoid using it unless your doctor specifically recommends it. People with Medical Conditions: If you have an autoimmune disease, seizure disorder, diabetes, depression, liver disease, or bleeding problems, talk to your doctor before taking melatonin. It may interact with blood thinners, diabetes medications, birth control pills, and immunosuppressants.
